what: Hydration is when JavaScript attaches event handlers and state to server-rendered HTML so it becomes interactive. Islands and resumability reduce that cost: islands hydrate only the interactive pieces, and resumable frameworks like Qwik skip replaying the app and load code only when an event happens.
like: Like a mostly printed poster with a few light switches: only the switches need wiring (islands), or the wiring is pre-labelled so it connects only when someone touches it (resumability).
why: Less JavaScript to download, parse and run, so pages become usable sooner
Main-thread work stays low, which helps INP on cheap phones
Static content stays static and cacheable

steps.d: The server sends a page the user can read at once. Everything after this is about how much JavaScript is needed to make it interactive.
Classic SSR frameworks re-run the whole component tree in the browser to attach handlers. web.dev warns this can hurt TBT and INP, even though FCP improves.

steps.t: Islands hydrate only what is marked
steps.d: In Astro a component renders to plain HTML with no JS unless it has a client directive. client:load hydrates at once, client:idle when the browser is idle, client:visible when it scrolls into view.
A server:defer component shows a fallback in the cached page, then its HTML is fetched separately and swapped in, so personalised parts do not make the whole page uncacheable.
Qwik serialises state and listeners into the HTML. A tiny global listener reads attributes like on:click and downloads the matching chunk only when the event fires.

numbers.l: of JavaScript a simple Qwik app needs to become interactive, per Qwik's own docs
hydration must restore on the client: listeners, the component tree and application state - what resumability avoids replaying
max length of an Astro server island GET URL; larger props switch to an uncacheable POST

choices.d: Content-heavy sites with a few widgets suit islands. Apps where most of the page is interactive gain little and may prefer streaming plus selective hydration.
load for above-the-fold critical widgets, idle for low priority, visible for below the fold, media for breakpoint-specific, only for client-only widgets with no SSR.
Islands are easy to adopt and framework-agnostic. Resumability gives finer lazy-loading but needs state to be serialisable and a different coding style.
Islands run in isolation, so share state with a small store or URL rather than props from a common parent.

instead.why: Stay in React and cut client JS by keeping most components on the server
Keep one app tree but hydrate boundary by boundary as it streams

breaks.d: Server and client render different output (dates, window checks, random values).
breaks.see: Console warnings, slowdown, handlers on wrong elements
breaks.fix: Make output deterministic; use suppressHydrationWarning for unavoidable text; use an effect for client-only content

breaks.d: Content is visible but the bundle is still hydrating, so clicks do nothing.
breaks.fix: Hydrate above-the-fold first, split bundles, defer low-priority islands

breaks.d: Large data passed into islands is serialised into the HTML.
breaks.fix: Pass ids, fetch inside the island, keep server island props small

say: Hydration has a cost: the browser must download and run the same code the server already ran. I would shrink that with islands or selective hydration so only interactive parts pay.
For a content site I would use islands, with client:visible for below-the-fold widgets, so most of the page ships zero JavaScript.
Resumability goes further by serialising state into HTML and loading code on the first event, at the price of writing serialisable, framework-specific code.

followups.q: Why not just use full SSR plus hydration everywhere?
followups.a: web.dev describes it as one app for the price of two: HTML plus duplicated data, and hydration work that can hurt TBT and INP. It is fine for small apps but costly as JS grows.

The client render differs from the server HTML, usually due to dates, browser-only checks or different data. React warns and may recover with slowdown; the fix is deterministic rendering or deferring client-only parts.

today: Partial hydration has gone mainstream: Astro ships islands and server islands, React uses Suspense-based selective hydration plus Server Components, and Qwik pushes resumability as an alternative to hydration.

check.q: In Astro, what happens to a component with no client directive?
check.a: It renders to HTML and CSS only, with no client JS
check.why: Zero JavaScript by default is the core of the islands model.

check.q: Which directive hydrates a component only when it enters the viewport?
What does Qwik do instead of hydration?
check.a: Serialises state and listeners into HTML and loads handler code on demand
check.why: Resumability continues where the server stopped.
